card.hook: Everyone leaves Venice with the same picture: that glowing neon-style sign, with a row of old arches lined up behind it like it's posing too. Good news, it's easy to get, and it looks great on a phone.
card.stand_here: Head to the corner of Pacific Avenue and Windward Avenue, then stand across Windward Avenue and face inland. You want the sign and arches filling the background, with the crowd behind you.
card.zoom: Stay on zoom 1x so the sign and arches look natural. Only drop to 0.5x if the pavement's too narrow to step back, and keep the sign away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the sign on one line, then tap the sign and slide the brightness a little darker so the neon colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the light comes from the east and the midday glare hasn't kicked in yet. Take a few frames between passing cars.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the crosswalk at Windward and Pacific, the classic Venice spot, with the sign overhead. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt the phone up so the sign sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Windward Avenue, facing inland, while you stand by the sign so it fills the shot behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Visitors are invited to photograph the Venice sign for personal use. It's a very busy junction, so wait for the green light before using the crosswalk, and don't step back into the road while you frame your shot.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the sign sitting on a gridline and not a single stranger's head in the frame. Bonus points if the arches line up perfectly.
card.good_to_know: Developer Abbot Kinney founded Venice in 1905 as a beach resort modelled on the Italian city, with canals, a pier and an arcaded business street. It was an independent city until 1926, when Los Angeles annexed it. Today the Ocean Front Walk promenade runs about 2.5 miles (4 km) and is lined with performers, fortune-tellers and vendors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the corner of Pacific Avenue and Windward Avenue, then stand across Windward Avenue and face inland. You want the sign and arches filling the background, with the crowd behind you.

card.hook: Picture a salt marsh. Now swap it for about 5,000 boats, all bobbing in one calm harbour. That's Marina del Rey, and it's a lot more photogenic than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Head to the waterfront lawn at Burton W. Chace Park, right on the marina's edge. The harbour area marked on the map is to the north-west of you, so face that way and look out over the boats.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to squeeze in the whole harbour, then drop to 1x for a calmer, more natural view. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat, a pier or the faraway hills.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the waterline on the lower or upper third, and use a pier or row of boats as a line leading into the picture.
card.best_time: Early morning gives you soft light, and sunset gives you a warm sky that reflects in the water. Weekends get busy, so an earlier start helps.
card.selfie_here: Try the pier at Burton W. Chace Park's sunset viewpoint, with the harbour channel behind you. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it on the front, and keep the boats and water over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you, go to the paved walkway at the end of Bora Bora, directly across from Fisherman's Village, and ask a passer-by to shoot you with the water and the lighthouse behind you, where there's a clearing and no boats in the way.
card.rules_and_safety: Parking at the park is paid and the lot can fill up at weekends. Some coastal paths in the area can be slippery in wet weather, so check conditions before you go.
card.challenge: Find the pier that leads your eye furthest, then see if you can catch the Palos Verdes hills at the end of it.
card.good_to_know: Marina del Rey is North America's largest man-made small-craft harbour, with slips for roughly 5,000 boats. Before it was built, this was a salt marsh fed by Ballona Creek. The harbour was formally dedicated on 10 April 1965.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the waterfront lawn at Burton W. Chace Park, right on the marina's edge. The harbour area marked on the map is to the north-west of you, so face that way and look out over the boats.

card.hook: There's no grand monument here, just sand, open sky and people getting on with their day. That's exactly why it makes such an easy, natural photo.
card.stand_here: Stand near Palawan Way, about 160 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west, and walk a little nearer if you want a closer shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the beach. Go to 0.5x for more sand and sky, or 2x to pick out a detail from where you stand.
card.make_it_pop: Bright sand can trick your phone into darkening everything, so tap on something mid-toned and slide to darker if the sand looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday. The beach may be quieter then too.
card.selfie_here: Try the selfie station next to the 7-foot soccer sculpture (4101 Admiralty Way). Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the sculpture over your shoulder. It was part of a June 12 to July 15 match-day event, so it may not be there now. Check the framing on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Lifeguards are on the beach during daylight hours. Check the official site before you go for any local rules or access restrictions.
card.challenge: Find a footprint trail in the sand and use it to lead the eye to a level horizon on one of your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Mother's Beach is a relaxed, everyday beach scene rather than a grand landmark. It sits within the Venice Beach map area, with the stand-here point on its north-east side. Map positions vary a little between sources, so confirm the exact spot on the map.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Palawan Way, about 160 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-west, and walk a little nearer if you want a closer shot.

selfie_spots.detail: at the selfie station next to the 7-foot soccer sculpture, which the page calls the centerpiece attraction at Mother's Beach (4101 Admiralty Way)
selfie_spots.why: It is the only page I found that names a dedicated selfie station at the beach, but the page does not say which way the beach faces in the frame, so check the framing on the spot.

Only one selfie spot was found, and no page names a spot with the whole beach in frame, so no photographer position is given; the photo-spot search found no specific angle. Map coordinates differ between sources: a Venice tourism page lists 33.9813536, -118.4599073, and a California Coastal Trail page lists 33.980540587313, -118.45898145, so confirm the exact spot on the map. No page gave selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: If people are training when you arrive, Muscle Beach Venice can hand you a ready-made action shot with the beach right behind it. If nobody is, the setting still gives your photos a strong sense of place.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Ocean Front Walk, about 75 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. From there you get the whole scene without standing in the middle of the crowd.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to take in the whole scene, then try zoom 0.5x if it's busy and you want more of the surroundings. Use zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like equipment or the shapes of the structures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the horizon level, and tap the main subject, then drag the slider to darker if the sky or sand looks too bright.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light, with the sun behind you. Early morning is generally quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the Venice Beach sign on Windward Avenue, the overhead 'Venice' lettering. Stand beneath it with the Muscle Beach side of the street behind you and use the front camera, or have someone shoot from across the street to fit the whole sign in. There's no fixed standing point for this one, so play around with where you stand.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed on the boardwalk, but ask before taking close-ups of individual athletes. Most people working out at the gym won't mind if you ask for a photo with them. Check any signs on site for access rules.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot to set the scene, then one close-up of a detail from the exact same spot, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: Muscle Beach Venice is on the Venice Beach seafront and appears to be an open public beachfront area. It's a busy public spot, so photos tend to work best when they include a bit of the surroundings. Keep strangers small in the frame by shooting from a little distance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Ocean Front Walk, about 75 m north-west of the subject, and face south-east. From there you get the whole scene without standing in the middle of the crowd.

selfie_spots.why: One blog presents the sign as a selfie stop and says a bonus is available for capturing the Muscle Beach backdrop, though the sources do not describe a fixed standing point for that.

card.hook: Imagine a little arched footbridge, bougainvillea spilling over it, and canal water so still the whole scene shows up twice. That's the corner you're hunting for, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Carroll Canal and Eastern Canal, where the two canal walkways meet. Face the footbridge so the bougainvillea frames it and the water reflects the houses and palms beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bridge, the flowers and the reflection in one shot. Then try 1x for a tidier, more natural look. If your phone has zoom 2x or 5x, use it to pick out one arch or some blossom, so you never need to step onto private ground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bougainvillea or the bridge, then slide it a touch darker so the flowers stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go when the canal is calm, because still water gives the best reflections. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is lovely on the flowers and the houses too.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the Grand Canal Court footbridge with the canal and houses behind you. Use the front camera (try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and let the canal fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Dell Avenue road bridge and aim west along Carroll Canal toward the Grand Canal Court footbridge, while you stand on the footbridge so you and the whole span are in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a residential historic district, so stay on the public walkways and don't block a bridge while you line up your shot. Keep away from private docks and yards, and leave residents out of close-ups. Some footbridges may be closed or worn, so check the official city information before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for the ripples to settle, then catch the bridge arch and its twin in the water in one calm frame.
card.good_to_know: Abbot Kinney built the Venice Canals as part of his Venice of California development. They're still fed with water from the Pacific through a tide gate at Ballona Lagoon. Some of the nine walking bridges are worn, and the city has no renovation plans for them.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Carroll Canal and Eastern Canal, where the two canal walkways meet. Face the footbridge so the bougainvillea frames it and the water reflects the houses and palms beside it.

selfie_spots.why: A Venice Beach visitor guide suggests taking a picture on a bridge with the canals in the background, which puts you in front of the canal footbridge landmark.

card.hook: Here's a little surprise in Los Angeles: still water, tiny footbridges and a whole second row of houses hanging upside down in the reflection. It feels like a different city, and it's a great place to take your time.
card.stand_here: Start at Carroll Canal Walk, about 150 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east, then stroll that way until a bridge or a bend in the canal sits in the middle distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the water, bridge and houses. Try zoom 0.5x on a narrow canal to get the whole bank and its reflection in one shot. If your phone has zoom 2x to 5x, use it for details like a footbridge, a garden or a reflection.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, so the reflection and the houses get about equal space.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and calmer reflections. The paths are usually quieter then too.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck a footbridge or a curve of the canal behind your shoulder. Hold the phone a little low and let the water show behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The homes here are private, so keep your phone pointed at the water and the bridges rather than into windows or gardens. Stick to the public walkways and follow any posted signs.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the upside-down houses in the water look even better than the real ones, then crouch a little and let the reflection fill the bottom half of your photo.
card.good_to_know: Developer Abbot Kinney built the canals in 1905 as part of his Venice of America, hoping to give this coast the feel of Venice, Italy. In 1929 many canals were filled in for roads, which cut thirteen canals down to six. The ones left were renovated in 1992 and re-opened in 1993.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at Carroll Canal Walk, about 150 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face south-east, then stroll that way until a bridge or a bend in the canal sits in the middle distance.

card.hook: Within ten steps you can spot a skater mid-turn, a volleyball flying over a net and a painted wall that's bigger than your living room. This strip does not do quiet, and that's why you'll love it.
card.stand_here: Stand near Speedway, about 660 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the whole promenade stretches out ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the long promenade and the crowd. Use 1x for everyday street scenes. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for skaters, performers and painted walls from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap your main subject, then slide the brightness down a little so the bright sand and sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and the light is soft. Late afternoon brings warm light over the sea. At midday it's the busiest, so expect lots of people crossing your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the boardwalk directly in front of the rainbow-painted Pride Lifeguard Tower, where Brooks Avenue meets the beach. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the tower over your shoulder, with white sand and blue ocean behind. Another option is the entrance to Gingerbread Court, on the boardwalk by the oceanfront.
card.ask_someone: At the end of Venice Beach Pier, ask a passer-by to face back toward the shore with your phone, so the coastline and boardwalk curve into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch for cyclists and skaters on the bike path, and keep your belongings close while you stop to shoot. Check the official site for local rules or closures before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a skater mid-turn: take a few frames in a row and see if you can spot the sharpest one.
card.good_to_know: The Venice Beach Boardwalk is a two-mile promenade that links up with the Santa Monica Boardwalk in the north and ends at Marina del Rey in the south. It draws roughly 10 million visitors a year, and Barbie and Nightcrawler were among the films shot here. Along the way you'll pass Muscle Beach Venice, the Venice Beach Skatepark and the Venice Art Walls.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Speedway, about 660 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From there the whole promenade stretches out ahead of you.

card.hook: Everyone flocks to Abbot Kinney Boulevard for the shopping, but the best backdrop is round the corner on a big, bold wall with way fewer people walking through your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Windward Avenue, near Abbot Kinney Boulevard, right in front of the 'Touch of Venice' mural. Face the wall and step back as far as the pavement allows.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x to fit the whole mural in when you're close to the wall, or 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. On the boulevard, 1x suits shopfronts, and zoom 2x to 5x picks out details across the street.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the mural's edges with them, then tap the mural and slide darker a touch if a bright wall or sky is washing out the colours.
card.best_time: Weekday mornings are quieter, so you're more likely to get a clear view of the wall and the street. Start with the mural, then head to the boulevard for wider street shots.
card.selfie_here: Head to the corner of Santa Clara Avenue and Abbot Kinney Boulevard and stand with J. Goldcrown's multicoloured hearts 'Love wall' behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more wall, and keep the hearts over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Street parking nearby is metered and strictly enforced, so read the signs before you leave your car. Murals can get repainted, so check recent photos to make sure the Love wall is still there.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole mural and one close-up of a small section, then see if friends can guess they're from the same wall.
card.good_to_know: Abbot Kinney Boulevard is a lively shopping street lined with storefronts, galleries and people. The 'Touch of Venice' mural is one of the area's most famous artworks, painted in a style that echoes the opening of a well-known 1958 film. If you drive, there's a flat-rate car park at Venice Boulevard and Electric Avenue.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Windward Avenue, near Abbot Kinney Boulevard, right in front of the 'Touch of Venice' mural. Face the wall and step back as far as the pavement allows.

selfie_spots.why: Guides name it as the most popular mural with tourists, and its heart-covered wall gives a colorful backdrop for a selfie.

card.hook: Picture a row of empty swimming pools, except people are rolling in and flying out of them on skateboards. That's Venice Beach Skatepark, and it's a great place to watch for a while.
card.stand_here: Stand near Speedway, about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stay on the public side of the edge, away from the riding area.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole park and its beachy surroundings, but it will look small. Try 2x for a better shot, or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one skater or one bowl from where you stand.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the skater and slide the picture a little darker so the pale concrete doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Morning is usually easiest, because the sun is behind you and lights up the park. Later in the day the low sun can shine toward your phone and cause glare.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera from the public side of the park's edge, with the bowls and skaters over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to fit more of the scene in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is free and open to the public, and its rules call for helmet and pad use. Keep your phone to the side, stay clear of the bowls and rails, and never step in front of a skater.
card.challenge: Wait for a skater to drop into a bowl, then catch the curve and the rider's pose together, with a slice of beach in the frame so it says Venice.
card.good_to_know: The park opened in late 2009 and is officially called the Dennis "Polar Bear" Agnew Memorial Skatepark, after a well-known skater. It covers about 16,000 square feet and mixes steps and rails with bowls. It was built after a long local campaign led by Jesse Martinez, and check the official site before you go for any current rules or closures.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Speedway, about 160 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stay on the public side of the edge, away from the riding area.

selfie_research.safety: <cite index="14-10">The park is free and open to the public, and its rules call for helmet and pad use.</cite>
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the skatepark behind the visitor, so I am returning none rather than guess. Pages do describe nearby areas that could work, but none says they are photo spots. The Cheese Wedge is <cite index="13-4">the circular area of skate obstacles, in between the board walk and the skate park</cite>, and a Stoked Ride page says <cite index="13-5">passerbys waiting to join the zoo of spectators at the skate park</cite> gather there. That is not a named photo position, so I left it out. The park address is <cite index="9-2">1800 Ocean Front Walk, Venice, CA</cite>, and the page lists coordinates close to yours. One travel guide calls the park a place for <cite index="11-5">epic sunset photography, with either the ocean as your backdrop or the bright shops that line the strand</cite>, but it does not name a spot on the sand or boardwalk. Also, the Venice Beach Skate Park is <cite index="16-5">right in the heart of Venice Beach, next to the graffiti walls, just past the basketball courts</cite>, which may help you find a viewpoint on site. No page I found mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, so I did not add any. The sources are mixed in age, and the 2018 and 2020 pages are older than the others.

card.hook: You're on the Southern California coast, but the painted wooden shops, white trim and a lighthouse say New England fishing village. It's a delightful, slightly confusing combo, and it photographs beautifully.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near Fiji Way, about 40 m south of the subject, and face north. You'll get the colourful fronts and some harbour in one shot without tilting your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the painted buildings, promenade and water together. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the lighthouse, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for masts, boat bows and signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the lighthouse straight, then tap a painted wall and slide a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the buildings. Midday sun can be harsh on the white trim and bright paint.
card.selfie_here: Go to Lighthouse Plaza and stand in front of the lighthouse tower with it behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the tower fits over your shoulder. For a marina look, walk along the harborfront promenade and put the sailboats behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask your photographer to stand a little back from the lighthouse in Lighthouse Plaza, while you stand in front of it, so the full tower and the colourful buildings fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The promenade is a public walking area, but individual businesses may have their own hours and rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Strike your best Bluth Banana Stand owner pose next to the lighthouse and get a friend to snap it.
card.good_to_know: Fisherman's Village has five brightly painted wooden buildings, a lighthouse, a fountain and a harbour promenade. The harbour is huge, with about 5,300 boats, yachts and commercial vessels across 21 marinas. Scenes with the Bluth Banana Stand from Arrested Development were filmed next to the lighthouse.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon near Fiji Way, about 40 m south of the subject, and face north. You'll get the colourful fronts and some harbour in one shot without tilting your phone up.

card.hook: Here's a fun fact about the Venice Sign: strangers will wander through your shot at exactly the wrong moment. Don't sweat it. Take a few pictures in a row and one of them will be clear.
card.stand_here: Stand near Windward Avenue, about 45 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there the sign is about 1 minute on foot, so you can fit it in with plenty of surroundings.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the sign and what's around it. Switch to 0.5x if you've got a group to squeeze in, or try 2x if you can't get any closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sign on your screen, then slide the brightness down a touch if the sky is bright and the sign looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, so you'll get fewer people in the frame. In the evening, switch on night mode if the light is low and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: For the classic one, stand in the middle of the Windward Avenue crosswalk at Windward and Pacific, with the sign straight above you. Use the front camera and 0.5x to fit it in. Want a more angled shot with palm trees beside the sign? Try the Pacific Avenue corner of the same intersection.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk across Windward Avenue from the sign, while you stand in front of it, so they can fit the full span in the frame (they can wait for a gap in the cars if you want the street clear beneath it).
card.rules_and_safety: Wait for the walk signal and a clear crossing before you step into the Windward and Pacific crosswalk, because cars come quickly once the light changes. Keep walkways clear for other people and stay out of traffic areas. Access isn't confirmed, so check locally before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on your gridlines and get one shot where the sign sits perfectly straight and not a single stranger walks through. Bonus points if you're smiling.
card.good_to_know: The Venice Sign is a photo spot on the Venice Beach map in Los Angeles, and it's great for a quick "I was here" picture. Its address is 80 Windward Ave. Take a few shots in case people walk through, and hold your phone upright to catch the sign's full height or sideways to get more of the surroundings.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Windward Avenue, about 45 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there the sign is about 1 minute on foot, so you can fit it in with plenty of surroundings.

card.hook: Picture a long grey road that forgot to stop and just kept going into the Pacific. That's Venice Fishing Pier, and the straight deck, railings and lamp posts do the composing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 160 m south-west of the subject, the Venice Fishing Pier, and face north-east. From here you see the whole pier, not just one chunk of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole pier and lots of sky in one shot, then try 1x for a natural look. Zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) picks out anglers, railings and waves around the pilings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the pier along a lower or upper third line so the deck leads the eye out to sea, and keep the horizon level because the ocean shows every tilt.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset is lovely, since the ocean is to the west. Early morning is usually quieter if you want fewer people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x so you and the pier both fit, and hold the phone a little high with the pier stretching out over your shoulder. Take a few, because the crowds and waves will keep moving behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone strap on and stay clear of the water's edge when waves are running. Check the official site before you go for current access arrangements and any restrictions.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the pier totally empty, then one with a few people in it on purpose. Which one makes the pier feel bigger?
card.good_to_know: The current pier dates from around 1963. It closed in the 1980s after storm damage and structural problems, then reopened in 1997 after a restoration. It's about 1,300 feet (roughly 400 metres) long, draws 28,000 to 30,000 visitors a day, and turned up in the 1993 thriller Falling Down.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 160 m south-west of the subject, the Venice Fishing Pier, and face north-east. From here you see the whole pier, not just one chunk of it.

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot or photo position was found for the Venice Beach, California pier (about 33.97778, -118.46917, at the pier's Washington Blvd end). The pages that discuss a selfie backdrop or a photo spot under the pier, such as visitsarasota.com and stephaniesnowphotography.com, describe the Venice Fishing Pier in Venice, Florida (Sharky's restaurant, Caspersen Beach), so I did not use them. The California-specific pages found (Yelp listing for 1 Washington Blvd, Marina Del Rey; mindtrip.ai; pierfishing.com) say only that the pier is good for sunset photos or photography in general, without naming a spot to stand or a spot to shoot from. Tim Gilbreath's location page mentions people under the pier and selfies on the shore, but does not say the location is in California, so I did not rely on it. No page gave rules on selfie sticks or tripods, or a safety point, for this pier. A search for a California-specific guide, such as a Venice Beach photo spots article that names the pier's north or south side or the beach below it, may turn up usable spots.

card.hook: Picture a pickup game in full swing, palm trees leaning overhead, a huge Californian sky and the beach just behind. That's the Venice Beach courts, and sometimes a helicopter drifts through the background for free.
card.stand_here: Stand about 850 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. When you reach the courts, the classic view looks south toward the handball courts, with the boardwalk and ocean behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the classic mix of courts, palms and sky. Drop to 0.5x to squeeze in the handball courts too, then try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for close shots of the players from the edge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the players, then drag the brightness slider a little darker so the bright sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Golden hour gives warm, dramatic light, and midday gives bright, clean colour. The courts have no lights, so shoot before sunset. On weekend afternoons people stand several deep along the fence, so get there early.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x so the courts and palms fit behind you, with the game over your shoulder. Stay off the playing area and let the players carry on.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the side of the playing area and let the game carry on around you. Check the official site before you go for any rules on use, events or filming.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photos, catch a jump shot mid-air, then scroll back and pick the frame where the ball is perfectly placed.
card.good_to_know: These open-air courts are widely described as the most photographed outdoor court in the world. They sit beside Ocean Front Walk, a 2.5-mile (4 km) promenade full of performers, fortune-tellers and vendors. Venice was founded in 1905 by Abbot Kinney as a seaside resort and became part of Los Angeles in 1926.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 850 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. When you reach the courts, the classic view looks south toward the handball courts, with the boardwalk and ocean behind you.

card.hook: Picture a big green lawn that ends in water on three sides, with boats bobbing everywhere and hardly a thing in the way. That's Burton Chace Park in Marina del Rey, and it's an easy one for a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand about 120 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. That puts lawn, water and sky in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the lawn, water and sky into one shot. Then go to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single boat or mast across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the brightest part of the sky so it keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the water and boats. Event days bring more people, so pick a quieter day if you want the lawns to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Head to the gazebo overlooking the marina and stand in or beside it, facing out over the water so the park is behind you. Use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the scene over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back along the entrance walkway off Mindanao Way, while you pose near the fountain and the Burton Chace plaque so the park is in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you spot sea lions, keep a respectful distance and don't disturb them. The docks and event areas may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a boat mast and line it up with one of your gridlines, then see if you can catch a tiny person relaxing on the lawn in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Burton Chace Park is the largest public park in Marina del Rey, at about 10 acres (4 hectares). It's named after Burton W. Chace, a former Mayor of Long Beach and Los Angeles County Supervisor. The green knoll in the middle gives a sweeping view across the harbour, and the park hosts events like the Marina del Rey Holiday Boat Parade, MarinaFest and the Marina Summer Concerts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 120 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. That puts lawn, water and sky in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a row of concrete walls on the sand, painted so many times that the colours and lettering you see today won't be there next month. That's the fun of the Venice Art Walls: every visit gives you a different picture.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ocean Front Walk, on the beach side at the corner of Windward Avenue, and face south-west. From here the walls are to the south-west and you see them at a slight angle, with the sand and beach spread out in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the walls, the sand and the beach into one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single mural or an artist at work.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest mural, then drag the slider down a touch to make the picture a little darker, so the colours stay rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Weekends are your best bet, because you can often watch artists adding new work. Murals tend to look freshest after a weekend, and late afternoon usually gives warm, softer light across the beach.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto the sand and stand in front of the painted walls, just west of the bike path and the Venice Skatepark. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a little low, so the wall fills the space behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the bike path on the Ocean Front Walk side, while you sit or stand in front of the walls so they catch the whole wall behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care near the beach bike path, where bikers and skaters move fast. Painting here is only for permitted artists and the rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Pick the wall with the boldest colour, take a close shot of it, then step back and take a wide one. Which one tells the better story?
card.good_to_know: People have been writing on these walls since the 1960s, though painting here only became properly legal in the last couple of decades. Since 2012 the walls have been managed by Setting the Pace, a graffiti production company that curates the work. It also runs mural workshops for students and young artists.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ocean Front Walk, on the beach side at the corner of Windward Avenue, and face south-west. From here the walls are to the south-west and you see them at a slight angle, with the sand and beach spread out in front of you.

card.hook: There's a Lighthouse Street Bridge here, and there has never been a lighthouse. What you get instead is still water, reeds and a quiet that feels a world away from the busy boardwalk nearby.
card.stand_here: Stand at midspan on the Lighthouse Street Bridge and face along the narrow channel towards the Venice Canals to the north-west. You'll have marsh and houses along the banks.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the channel and the banks. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the bridge's arch in the shot, for example from the trail. For birds, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) and don't walk closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the channel up with a vertical grid line so the water leads the eye into the picture.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the water and fewer people. Mid-tide or high tide tends to look best, because the water covers more of the mud.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the bridge deck at the top of the span with the lagoon behind you, use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to fit in more water. For a second spot, use the west bank trail about 0.1 mi north of the bridge crossing, at the History of Ballona Lagoon marker.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Pacific Avenue sidewalk at Lighthouse Street to aim at the bridge while you stand on it.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is for pedestrians and bikes only. Stay outside any fenced nesting areas on the beach next door, and wear comfy shoes because some stretches of path are unpaved.
card.challenge: Spot a snowy egret or a great blue heron at the water's edge, then tap it on screen and get the shot before it strolls off.
card.good_to_know: The bridge is a vintage arched one, built by Abbot Kinney as part of his Venice of California development. The lagoon was restored from the late 1980s, with major work in 1996-97, which brought back native plants and bird habitat. The streets around here are named after nautical terms in alphabetical order.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at midspan on the Lighthouse Street Bridge and face along the narrow channel towards the Venice Canals to the north-west. You'll have marsh and houses along the banks.
